# Use a standard Ubuntu base image suitable for CPU builds
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Set environment variables to enable non-interactive installation
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Install build dependencies, git, cmake, OpenMPI, and certificates.
# Open MPI is essential for this HPC application.
# ca-certificates are required for git to clone from https repositories securely.
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    ca-certificates \
    cmake \
    g++ \
    git \
    libopenmpi-dev \
    openmpi-bin \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Clone the Kripke source code from the master branch into /opt/kripke.
# Correction: The repository's primary branch is 'master', not 'main'.
# We use --recurse-submodules to fetch required dependencies like BLT.
# We use --depth 1 for a shallow clone to reduce image size.
RUN git clone --depth 1 --recurse-submodules --branch master https://github.com/LLNL/kripke.git /opt/kripke

# Set the working directory to the cloned repository for the build process
WORKDIR /opt/kripke

# Configure and build Kripke using CMake
# A separate build directory is created to keep the source tree clean.
# Flags are set for a release build with MPI and OpenMP enabled, typical for HPC CPU applications.
# The build is parallelized using all available processor cores to speed up image creation.
RUN mkdir build && \
    cd build && \
    cmake \
      -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -D ENABLE_MPI=ON \
      -D ENABLE_OPENMP=ON \
      .. && \
    make -j$(nproc)

# Copy the compiled executable to a system location on the PATH.
# This makes the 'kripke' command available system-wide.
RUN cp /opt/kripke/build/bin/kripke.exe /usr/local/bin/kripke

# Clean up the build environment to reduce the final image size.
# The source code is no longer needed in the production image.
RUN rm -rf /opt/kripke

# Set the default working directory for when the container starts.
WORKDIR /

# Default command to execute when the container runs.
# This displays the help message, which is useful for verifying the build
# and discovering runtime options. In a real Kubernetes deployment, this
# command would be overridden by the MPI operator or user-provided arguments.
CMD ["kripke", "--help"]

# MiniCluster manifest for running the Kripke benchmark on AWS CPU instances.
# This manifest is designed for the Flux Operator in Kubernetes.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Name of the MiniCluster instance
  name: kripke-mci-aws-cpu
  # Target namespace for deployment
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The total number of pods in the MiniCluster (the job size)
  # Set to 1 to run on a single node as requested.
  size: 1

  # The total number of tasks to run across the MiniCluster.
  # Flux will run this many copies of the command.
  tasks: 4

  # Defines the application container to run within the Flux overlay network.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:kripke
      # The command to be executed by Flux.
      # The Flux Operator wraps this command in `flux run`, so it should not be included here.
      # This is a sample command for Kripke for a small-scale run.
      command: kripke --groups 1 --zones 1,1,1 --niter 10
      # Per instructions, this container is not the launcher pod.
      # The Flux Operator will designate the broker pod (rank 0) as the launcher.
      launcher: false
      # This container will participate in the flux instance
      runFlux: true

  # Logging settings for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    # Strict mode ensures that if a log stream can't be created, the job fails.
    strict: true

  # Job completion policies.
  # Do not automatically clean up pods and services upon job completion.
  # This is useful for debugging and inspecting logs/results.
  cleanup: false

# MiniCluster manifest for running the Kripke benchmark, optimized for a single AWS Graviton (ARM) instance.
# This version corrects application parameters and targets a specific high-performance node type.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Name of the MiniCluster instance
  name: kripke-mci-aws-cpu
  # Target namespace for deployment
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The total number of pods in the MiniCluster (the job size).
  # Set to 1 to run on a single node as requested.
  size: 1

  # The total number of tasks to run across the MiniCluster.
  # Increased to 64 to fully utilize the cores of the target hpc7g.16xlarge instance.
  tasks: 64

  # Do not automatically clean up pods and services upon job completion for debugging.
  cleanup: false

  # Logging settings for the Flux Operator.
  logging:
    # Strict mode ensures that if a log stream can't be created, the job fails.
    strict: true

  # Pod spec additions to control scheduling.
  pod:
    # Ensures the MiniCluster pods are scheduled only on nodes with this specific instance type label.
    nodeSelector:
      node.kubernetes.io/instance-type: hpc7g.16xlarge

  # Flux-specific overrides.
  flux:
    container:
      # Specifies the ARM64-compatible Flux container image, required for AWS Graviton instances.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-view-rocky:arm-9

  # Defines the application container to run within the Flux overlay network.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:kripke
      # Corrected command: --groups is set to 2 to be divisible by the default number of groupsets (2).
      command: kripke --groups 2 --zones 1,1,1 --niter 10
      # This container will participate in the flux instance.
      runFlux: true
      # This container is not the launcher pod.
      launcher: false

  # Target namespace for deployment

  # The total number of pods in the MiniCluster (the job size).

  size: 1

  tasks: 64

    strict: true

  pod:

    container:

      launcher: false

      launcher: false

This attempt will test a hybrid MPI+OpenMP configuration (16 tasks x 4 threads) on the same high-performance hardware. This is a standard HPC optimization technique intended to reduce MPI communication overhead and improve cache utilization, which may lead to a higher Grind Time Figure of Merit.

The previous hybrid MPI+OpenMP attempt on ARM resulted in a major performance regression compared to the initial pure-MPI run. This attempt reverts to the more successful pure-MPI strategy and switches to a different high-performance architecture (AMD EPYC via c7a.12xlarge) to explore potential architectural advantages. The process layout is adjusted to fully utilize the 48 available cores.

The previous attempt achieved the best performance so far by switching to an AMD EPYC node (c7a.12xlarge) with a pure-MPI strategy. This attempt will now test a hybrid MPI+OpenMP configuration on this same high-performing hardware. By using fewer MPI processes (12) and multiple threads per process (4), we aim to reduce communication overhead and improve cache utilization, which could further increase the Figure of Merit.

Previous results show a pure-MPI strategy on the AMD c7a.12xlarge instance is the current optimum, vastly outperforming ARM and hybrid MPI+OpenMP configurations. This attempt will test the same winning pure-MPI strategy on the highest-core-count Intel instance available (c6i.16xlarge) to determine if Intel's architecture provides a performance advantage over AMD for this workload.

The analysis indicates a clear optimum has been reached. Attempt #3 on the AMD `c7a.12xlarge` node with a pure-MPI strategy (48 tasks) yielded the highest Figure of Merit (3.704748e-05). Subsequent attempts with hybrid MPI+OpenMP on the same hardware, or pure-MPI on different architectures (Intel, ARM), resulted in lower performance. Further tuning of application-level parameters like process grid decomposition is unlikely to produce a significant improvement over this established baseline.
